learningObjectives.title: Basic probability and the probability scale

questions.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain to happen?
questions.explain: An event that is certain has a probability of 1, the maximum on the probability scale.

questions.q: The probability scale ranges from which values?
questions.explain: All probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

questions.q: The probability that event A does NOT happen is equal to:
questions.explain: Because all outcomes sum to 1, the probability of 'not A' is 1 minus P(A).

questions.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it does not rain?
Two events are described as mutually exclusive if:
options: they cannot both happen at the same time
questions.explain: Mutually exclusive events have no common outcomes, so they cannot occur simultaneously.

questions.q: For two mutually exclusive events A and B, P(A or B) is equal to:
questions.explain: For mutually exclusive events the probabilities are simply added together.

questions.q: Relative frequency (experimental probability) is calculated as:
options: number of successful trials / total number of trials
total number of trials / number of successful trials
questions.explain: Relative frequency is the number of times an outcome occurs divided by the total number of trials.

questions.q: To obtain a more reliable estimate of an experimental probability, you should:
questions.explain: As the number of trials increases, relative frequency gives a better estimate of the true probability.

questions.q: The expected number of times an event occurs is found by:
questions.explain: Expected frequency equals the probability of the event multiplied by the number of trials.

questions.q: A fair dice is rolled 300 times. The probability of rolling a six is 1/6. How many sixes would you expect?
questions.explain: Expected sixes = 1/6 x 300 = 50.

questions.q: A coin is spun 60 times and lands on heads 27 times. What is the relative frequency of heads?
questions.explain: Relative frequency = 27 / 60 = 0.45.

questions.q: A sample space diagram is used to:
options: list all possible outcomes of one or more events
questions.explain: A sample space diagram systematically shows every possible outcome of the combined events.

questions.q: When two ordinary six-sided dice are rolled, the total number of possible outcomes is:
questions.explain: Each die has 6 outcomes, so combined there are 6 x 6 = 36 outcomes.

questions.q: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the totals equals 7?
questions.explain: There are 6 ways to make 7 out of 36 outcomes, giving 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.q: On a tree diagram, to find the probability of a sequence of events along one path you:
options: multiply the probabilities along the branches
add the probabilities along the branches
subtract the probabilities along the branches
divide the probabilities along the branches
questions.explain: Probabilities are multiplied along the branches of a single path through a tree diagram.

questions.q: Events A and B are independent. Then P(A and B) is equal to:
questions.explain: For independent events the probability of both occurring is the product of their probabilities.

questions.q: A counter is drawn from a bag and replaced, then a second is drawn. P(red) = 0.2 each time. What is the probability that both counters are red?
questions.explain: The picks are independent, so P(both red) = 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04.

questions.q: On a Venn diagram, the intersection of sets A and B represents outcomes that are:
questions.explain: The intersection contains the outcomes common to both sets A and B.

questions.q: In set notation, A union B (A ∪ B) represents outcomes that are in:
questions.explain: The union of two sets contains every outcome in A, in B, or in both.

questions.q: For a set of exhaustive events, the individual probabilities must:
questions.explain: Exhaustive events cover all possibilities, so their probabilities sum to 1.
